title: When to travel for the Great Migration
excerpt: The herds move with the rain, not the calendar. Here is how the year usually unfolds across the Mara and Serengeti, and what to plan around.

content.heading: The movement follows the rain
content.body: The migration is a response to grass and water, which means its timing shifts from year to year. Any honest answer starts there: no month guarantees a river crossing. What can be planned is where the herds are most likely to be, and which camps offer the best access when they arrive.

content.heading: Early in the year: the southern plains
content.body: Calving usually takes place on the southern Serengeti plains in the early months, when short grass and minerals draw the herds together. Predator activity around the calving grounds is high, and the landscape is at its most open.

content.heading: The middle of the year: north and west
content.body: As the grass dries, the herds move west along the corridor and then north toward the Mara River. This is the period most associated with crossings — dramatic, unpredictable, and best viewed with a guide who has spent the season on that stretch of river.

content.heading: The other months
content.body: Outside the movement, the Mara and Serengeti remain excellent. Resident game stays, grass is shorter and easier to read, and camps are quieter and often better value. For a first safari focused on cats rather than crowds, the quieter months are worth serious consideration.

title: A first-timer’s guide to the Swahili coast
excerpt: Stone Town, spice farms, dhow sailing and reef water: how to shape a few days on the coast without rushing any of it.

content.heading: Start with the town
content.body: Stone Town rewards walking. The carved doors, the coral-rag walls and the market are best seen early, before the heat, with someone who lives there. Two nights is enough for the town and a spice farm; an afternoon is not.

content.heading: Then choose your coast
content.body: The north has the liveliest water and the easiest swimming. The east is quieter, with a bigger tidal range and a slower rhythm. Both are beautiful; they suit different travellers.

content.heading: Tides structure the day
content.body: On much of the coast the water retreats a long way, twice a day. Plan snorkelling and sailing around the tide tables rather than around a fixed schedule, and keep the middle of the day for shade.

content.heading: Travel with respect
content.body: Zanzibar is a conservative Muslim society. Away from the beach, cover shoulders and knees, ask before photographing people, and buy directly from makers where you can.

title: Packing for a family safari
excerpt: Light aircraft limits, cold mornings, dusty afternoons and long days in a vehicle: what actually earns its place in the bag.

content.heading: Soft bags, small weights
content.body: Bush flights usually cap luggage at 15kg per person in a soft bag. This is the constraint that decides everything else — pack for it at home, not at the airstrip.

content.heading: Layers beat coats
content.body: Mornings in an open vehicle can be genuinely cold, and by midday you will want short sleeves. Thin layers, a warm fleece and a light windproof shell cover almost every case.

content.heading: Neutral colours, and no bright white
content.body: Muted tones work better for wildlife and for dust. Avoid camouflage patterns, which are restricted in several countries, and bring a hat that stays on in wind.

content.heading: For children
content.body: Bring their own binoculars if possible, a refillable bottle each, and something to do during the middle of the day. A private vehicle makes the pace far easier to manage.
